text: Every school in America has a lockdown drill. You learn it in kindergarten, the same way you learn your address. Lights off. Lock the door. Cover the window. Get in the corner away from the door. Phones on silent. And the most important rule of all: you don't open that door for anyone. Not a teacher, not a friend, not your own mom. When it's really over, someone with a key will open it for you. I've done that drill maybe forty times. And on October twelfth, at ten fourteen in the morning, in Room 214, I found out why that last rule exists. Third period, English. Ms. Harlow was reading Poe out loud. Tyler was drawing on his arm. Priya, who sits next to me, was actually taking notes. And then the speaker over the door clicked on.

text: They had keys. They didn't knock, and they didn't ask. They walked us out single file, hands on the shoulder of the person in front. And as we went down the hall, I looked into Room 208. The door was wide open. Every backpack was still on its desk. A water bottle was rolling slowly on the floor. Nobody was in there. On the stairs, I counted the open doors on our floor. Five. Five rooms that heard someone they trusted and did exactly what any normal person would do. Nobody from those rooms was outside with us. Nobody from those rooms was ever found. Outside, it was chaos. Parents, police, news vans. I heard a deputy telling Ms. Harlow they'd checked every security camera in the building, and all day long, the second-floor hallway was empty. No one walking. No one knocking. Just doors, rattling, one by one, on their own. They sat us all in the gym across the street, and a lady from the district with a clipboard asked every single one of us the same question. "Did anyone in your room open the door?" Not "are you okay." Not "what did you see." Just that. And every time someone said no, she let out this tiny breath and wrote something down, and I remember thinking, she knows. Whatever this is, she's seen it before. And then my mom came through the crowd and grabbed me so hard she lifted me off the ground, and for the first time all day I let myself breathe. It was over. We'd done everything right. We never opened the door.
